protagonist: Priya Nathan, Treasury/Reserves Analyst, Northlight Financial (fictional stablecoin issuer)

deliverables.text: A scientific-notation reserve table: write Northlight's total reserve amount in scientific notation, then compute and write each option's total annual dollar yield in scientific notation, showing every intermediate step.

An absolute-value peg-deviation worksheet: for each of Appendix D's five price snapshots, compute |price - $1.00| in dollars, convert to basis points, and label each 'small' or 'historically large' against Appendix E's reference deviations.

A yield-per-risk efficiency table: for both options, divide D1's annual dollar yield by the option's duration-scaled peg-deviation figure in basis points (Appendix E), and state the percent difference between the two options.

A sensitivity check: recompute D3's efficiency table using Appendix E's alternate scaling readings for Option B's risk figure (linear duration scaling, and a 'no extra risk' floor case), and state whether the recommendation changes under each.
A recommendation memo defended with D1's dollar figures, D3/D4's efficiency numbers, and Appendix A's hard constraint that both ladders already sit inside the GENIUS Act's legal ceiling.

balance.argument_a: The Short Ladder keeps every dollar of the reserve within about two weeks of maturity, on average -- close to the real, disclosed posture of the actual money-market fund backing a major real dollar stablecoin (Appendix B, S2). Its peg-deviation reference is a real, documented figure (30 bps, normal high-volatility-hour drift, S5), and D3's efficiency figure (~$91.8 million of annual yield per basis point of duration-scaled risk) is meaningfully larger than the Extended Ladder's under the primary, industry-standard square-root-of-time reading -- by 17.04%, safely inside SPEC §2's ~20% cap.
balance.argument_b: The Extended Ladder is still entirely legal -- both options sit well inside the GENIUS Act's 93-day ceiling (Appendix A, S7) -- and it earns a real, recurring $44.1 million more per year (D1) on a reserve this size, for only 1.5x the average time-to-maturity of the Short Ladder. Using the same real, industry-standard duration-scaling methodology (S9) that favors Option A under its primary reading, a Hero can point out that D4's sensitivity check shows the case is genuinely close: a different, also-defensible scaling assumption (linear rather than square-root) widens the gap, but the most conservative defensible reading (no incremental duration risk) actually flips the recommendation to Option B outright. That volatility in the verdict itself is the argument for B -- the real data does not decisively rule it out.
balance.margin_basis: For each option: annual dollar yield (reserve total x yield rate, Appendix A/B/C) divided by that option's duration-scaled peg-deviation reference in basis points (Appendix E) gives dollars of annual yield earned per basis point of peg-deviation risk shouldered. Option A's reference deviation is a real, sourced figure (30 bps, S5). Option B's reference deviation is that same real figure scaled to Option B's own Treasury-bill duration via the square-root-of-time rule (S9): dev_B_bps = dev_A_bps x sqrt(duration_B_days / duration_A_days). margin_pct is the percent difference between the two options' efficiency figures under this primary (square-root-of-time) reading.
balance.margin_note: COMPUTED 2026-09-01 (case-redesign pass, balance retune). ORIGINAL DESIGN (superseded): Option A (4-week bills) vs. Option B (13-week bills), Option A's risk reference = 30 bps (real normal drift, S5) vs. Option B's risk reference = 1,224 bps (real March 2023 USDC/SVB crisis tick-low, S1) -- an apples-to-oranges comparison of a normal-conditions figure against a catastrophic tail event. That design produced margin_pct = 97.47% (96.9%-97.8% across all three real sourced readings of the crisis event), far past SPEC §2's ~20% cap, and was flagged, not self-waived, in the original RESEARCH_LOG.md. REDESIGNED (this pass): the dilemma is retuned to Option A (4-week bills, 28-day average tenor) vs. Option B (6-week bills, 42-day average tenor) -- a closer, still-meaningfully-different pair (lever (a) from the retune brief) -- AND the risk metric is retuned to compare BOTH options on the SAME real reference figure (30 bps normal drift, S5), scaled to each option's own duration by the square-root-of-time rule (S9), the real, Basel-Committee-recommended method for scaling a risk estimate across holding horizons -- rather than mixing a normal-conditions figure for one option with a crisis figure for the other (lever from the retune brief: 'reframe the risk side of the metric so both options are measured on the same kind of risk, scaled by something that actually differs proportionally between the options'). ARITHMETIC: reserve_total = $73,434,000,000 (S1). annual_yield_A = 73,434,000,000 x 0.0375 = $2,753,775,000 (S6). annual_yield_B = 73,434,000,000 x 0.0381 = $2,797,835,400 (S6). extra_yield_B_over_A = $44,060,400/yr. dev_A_bps = 30 (S5). duration_A_days = 28, duration_B_days = 42 (Appendix B/C). scaling_factor = sqrt(42/28) = sqrt(1.5) = 1.224744871... dev_B_bps (primary) = 30 x 1.224744871 = 36.742346 bps. efficiency_A = 2,753,775,000 / 30 = $91,792,500 per bp. efficiency_B (primary) = 2,797,835,400 / 36.742346 = $76,147,434.60 per bp. margin_pct = (91,792,500 - 76,147,434.60) / 91,792,500 x 100 = 17.04%. WINNER: Option A, The Short Ladder, by 17.04% -- under SPEC §2's ~20% cap. SENSITIVITY (full detail in RESEARCH_LOG.md and sensitivity_model.py): swapping the scaling methodology for dev_B_bps across three real, defensible readings changes the outcome meaningfully -- (1) square-root-of-time [primary, S9]: dev_B = 36.74 bps, margin = 17.04%, Option A wins; (2) linear/proportional-to-duration scaling [alternate]: dev_B = 45.00 bps, margin = 32.27%, Option A wins more decisively; (3) no incremental duration risk [floor case, not realistic but a defensible lower bound]: dev_B = 30.00 bps (same as A), margin = 1.57%, Option B actually wins. The case's own D4 deliverable walks a Hero through exactly this sweep. Context check (not part of the graded metric, kept as background/facilitator color): if Option B had instead been the original 13-week ladder, the same square-root-of-time methodology gives dev_B = 30 x sqrt(91/28) = 54.08 bps, efficiency_B = $52,546,671.93/bp, margin = 42.75% -- explaining, using the case's own real methodology, why Priya's actual draft never went all the way to the legal maximum.

modeling_assumptions.claim: Appendix D/E's 'normal drift' figure (30 bps) is sourced to USDT specifically, applied here as Option A's real reference deviation and as the base figure Option B's risk-scaled deviation is derived from
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public figure exists for a fictional company; the sourced figure describes real stablecoin behavior generally and is the best available real analog.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: REVISED IN THIS REDESIGN: no longer load-bearing for margin_pct at all. Because Option B's deviation is now derived as dev_A_bps x (a fixed scaling factor, MA3), this base figure cancels out of the ratio between eff_A and eff_B exactly the same way reserve_total does (MA4) -- changing it moves both options' displayed efficiency numbers up or down together but never changes which option wins or by how much. It remains load-bearing only for D1/D2/D3's displayed dollar-per-bp figures, not for the balance verdict. (In the original, pre-redesign version of this case, this figure WAS load-bearing, because Option B's deviation was an independent, unrelated crisis-event figure rather than a scaled derivative of this one.)

modeling_assumptions.claim: Option B's peg-deviation risk reference is derived by scaling Option A's real reference deviation (MA2) to Option B's own Treasury-bill duration via the square-root-of-time rule -- the same method (recommended by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision) used industry-wide to scale a risk/volatility estimate from a shorter holding horizon to a longer one
modeling_assumptions.value: dev_B_bps = dev_A_bps x sqrt(duration_B_days / duration_A_days) = 30 x sqrt(42/28) = 36.74 bps (primary reading)
modeling_assumptions.basis: S9 (Daniellsson & Zigrand, LSE, 2003), confirming the real formula and its real Basel-Committee endorsement. Chosen over the original design's approach (comparing a normal-drift figure for one option against an unrelated historical crisis-event figure for the other) because it measures both options on the SAME kind of risk -- interest-rate/duration exposure -- scaled by something that genuinely differs between the two options (their Treasury-bill maturity), rather than mixing two different risk categories.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: HIGH -- this is now the single assumption the whole balance computation turns on, replacing the original design's MA3 (which historical crisis reading to use). Swept across three real, defensible scaling choices: square-root-of-time [primary, S9's own recommended method] gives margin_pct = 17.04% (Option A wins, under the ~20% cap); linear/proportional-to-duration scaling [S9 itself discusses this as an alternative] gives margin_pct = 32.27% (Option A wins more decisively); a 'no incremental duration risk' floor case (not a realistic assumption, but a defensible lower bound establishing that duration risk cannot be negative) gives margin_pct = 1.57% and actually FLIPS the winner to Option B. This is disclosed plainly, not hidden -- see D4 and RESEARCH_LOG.md. S9's own paper additionally notes the square-root-of-time rule tends to UNDERestimate risk for longer or fatter-tailed horizons relative to a jump-diffusion process -- meaning the case's primary reading, if anything, may be mildly favorable to Option B (the longer-duration option), not stacked against it.

modeling_assumptions.claim: Reserve total is a live, moving market figure, frozen at a single as-of date
modeling_assumptions.basis: Per SPEC Sec 5's rule on citing a still-changing real quantity: every live figure in this case (reserve total, both Treasury yields) is frozen at the same single date, stated explicitly.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not change margin_pct -- the reserve total cancels out of the dollars-per-basis-point ratio (D3), since it multiplies both options' annual-yield figures identically. Load-bearing only for D1's absolute dollar figures.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: This exponent (0=no incremental risk, 0.5=square-root-of-time, 1.0=linear duration scaling) is computed from a validated scaling relationship, not guessed: S9 (Daniellsson & Zigrand, LSE, 2003) confirms the square-root-of-time formula AND explicitly discusses the linear alternative and the zero-scaling floor case as the same relationship's other defensible readings -- the +-50% flex (0.25 to 0.75) stays fully inside the range S9's own paper discusses, not extrapolated past it. A +50% flex (exponent 0.75, between sqrt and linear) pushes margin to 33.4%, over SPEC Sec 2's ~20% cap -- this is already the case's own central, plainly-disclosed finding (see balance.margin_note, sensitivity_note, and FACILITATOR.md's Anchor 4/Twist/Deep-conflict sections), not a new discovery. The case does not hide this: it is built around exactly this instability being the point of D4 and the Twist.

sensitivity_note: margin_pct (17.04%) is driven entirely by MA3 -- which real, defensible risk-scaling methodology is used to derive Option B's duration-scaled deviation figure from Option A's real 30 bps base. The primary reading (square-root-of-time, the real Basel-Committee-recommended method, S9) lands margin_pct safely under SPEC Sec 2's ~20% cap, but a different real, also-defensible reading (linear duration scaling) widens the margin to 32.27%, and an unrealistic 'no incremental risk' floor case flips the winner to Option B entirely (margin 1.57%). This sensitivity is disclosed plainly and is the substance of the case's own D4 deliverable, not a defect being hidden -- see RESEARCH_LOG.md's redesign section and sensitivity_model.py's full sweep. (For contrast: the original, pre-redesign version of this case had margin_pct = 97.47%, driven by mixing a normal-drift reference for Option A against an unrelated historical-crisis reference for Option B -- see RESEARCH_LOG.md for the full retune history.)
